name: Shift
tagline: iPhone focus tool that restricts distracting apps with OS level controls that are hard to undo on impulse.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The blocking mechanics here are Apple's, not proprietary: FamilyControls, ManagedSettings and DeviceActivity let any developer shield chosen apps and run schedules, and an agent can wire that into a small SwiftUI app quickly. The gaps are all logistics, not logic: you need a Mac, Xcode, a physical device because the simulator does not support these frameworks, and a paid Apple Developer account unless you enjoy resigning the build every seven days. The harder tier, actual supervised device management that survives you deleting the blocker in a moment of weakness, means running a real MDM server and supervising the phone, which is a different and much less pleasant project. So a personal version that shields apps on a schedule with a deliberate friction delay is a weekend, and a version you genuinely cannot defeat at 11pm is not. That last part is the whole product for most buyers.
coreLoopDIY: A local SwiftUI app that lets you pick apps and categories, shields them on a schedule or on demand, and forces a countdown plus a typed confirmation before anything unlocks early.
requirements: A Mac with a recent Xcode
An iPhone on iOS 16 or later, physical device required
Apple Developer account if you want the build to last longer than 7 days
Family Controls capability enabled on the app target
Screen Time authorization granted on device
whatYouLose: Restrictions that survive you deleting the app, which is the part that actually changes behavior
Supervision and device management setup done for you instead of you hosting anything
Polished onboarding, presets and shield screens that do not look like a debug build
Cross device and cross platform coverage, iPad and Mac included
Someone else keeping it alive through iOS releases that quietly change Screen Time behavior
moatNotes: The real asset is knowing where Apple's Screen Time APIs and device management paths break, and having the entitlements and setup flow to work around it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Self control tools only work when the escape hatch is inconvenient, and a blocker you wrote yourself is the easiest thing in the world to disable: you know exactly where the off switch is, and you can just delete the target from Xcode. Paying for it buys a stranger's restrictions, a setup flow that puts the controls somewhere you cannot casually reach, and maintenance across iOS updates that periodically change how shielding behaves. It is one of the rare categories where the friction is the feature and DIY undermines it by construction.
notes: You can rebuild the mechanism in a weekend; the hard part is building something your future self cannot talk out of.
prompt:
Build a personal iOS app called Focus Shield that blocks distracting apps using Apple's Screen Time frameworks.

Stack: Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI, single Xcode project, iOS 17 minimum. No backend, no accounts, no analytics, no third party packages.

Targets and capabilities:
- Main app target with the Family Controls capability.
- A DeviceActivityMonitor extension target for schedule start and end callbacks.
- A ShieldConfiguration extension so blocked apps show a custom shield with a short message.
- Shared App Group for state between app and extensions.

Features in scope:
1. On first launch, request Screen Time authorization with AuthorizationCenter, individual enrollment. Show a clear failure state if denied.
2. A screen using FamilyActivityPicker to select apps, categories and web domains. Persist the FamilyActivitySelection to the App Group via Codable in UserDefaults.
3. Apply shields with ManagedSettingsStore: applicationCategories, applications and webDomains from the saved selection.
4. Schedules: let the user define named windows (weekday mornings, evenings, custom) with start and end times and day of week toggles. Register them with DeviceActivityCenter and apply or clear shields in the monitor extension.
5. A manual Focus Now button with a duration picker that shields immediately and auto clears when time is up.
6. Friction to unlock early: a 60 second countdown plus typing a fixed phrase stored in .env style config baked at build time, then and only then clear the store. No skip button.
7. A simple local log of sessions and early unlocks, stored in the App Group, shown as a plain list. No charts.

Out of scope, do not build: iCloud or any sync, an accountability partner, MDM or device supervision, App Store metadata, push notifications beyond local notifications for session end, paywalls, telemetry.

Deliverables: the Xcode project, a README that lists the exact capabilities to enable, the App Group identifier to set, why a physical device is required, and the fact that a free provisioning profile expires after 7 days. Include the unlock phrase in a single Config.swift constant and note it in the README so it is easy to change and easy to make annoying.
